en: The Essential Gate to the Contemplation of the Pure Land Realm,
originally transmitted through the Tiantai school,
composed by the Dharma Master Xingjiao, the Tiger Valley Śramaṇa Huaize.
Now, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is the essential path for sentient beings of the末代 (final age) to transcend birth and death;
it is the vessel that cuts across the five realms of existence.
Once born there, they shall never again fall back;
with their celestial bodies, they travel with sovereign ease,
and food and clothing are obtained spontaneously.
May the assembly of beings in the ocean of purity always behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma, swiftly entering the ranks of the noble ones,
and be free from the afflictions of tigers, wolves, lions, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice, as well as all other sentient beings that cause harm.
There is no affliction from cold, heat, wind, rain, or the torments of insentient things.
One is born by transformation within a lotus flower with an immeasurable lifespan.
Since there is no suffering such as birth, old age, sickness, or death, one experiences only various forms of bliss.
Therefore, it is named the World of Ultimate Bliss.
Thus, I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, desire to cause the sentient beings of this land who are lost in delusion to escape from all sufferings by opening the gate of subduing them.
The Compassionate Father Amitābha reveals the path of compassionate acceptance;
it is for this reason that he speaks with such bitter earnestness and diligent exhortation,
praising the Pure Land exclusively and universally encouraging rebirth therein.
Therefore, among the sages and worthies, as well as the monastics and laity, of India and this land,
those who dedicated their merit and made vows to behold the Buddha at the time of death and attain rebirth in his pure land are fully recorded in the scriptures and chronicles, beyond counting.
However, inferior ordinary beings greedily cling to coarse and base forms and sounds,
willingly wandering through birth and death without seeking liberation.
They are like those who have entered a city and taken up their posts.
If one does not prepare a place to rest in advance,
and finds oneself with no lodging by the time evening falls,
it is deeply pitiable and lamentable.
However, among those superior and virtuous people,
many are weary of suffering and seek happiness, giving rise to the aspiration to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
yet few understand the contemplation of the objective realm.
I have therefore taken up my brush to briefly record the general outline,
hoping that those who possess faith and joy may,
by means of this, find the gateway to entering the Way.
One shall not labor in vain through ascetic practices. Upon first entering the *maṇḍala*, one should maintain the visualization of the Three Jewels.
With a heart of sincere compassion, one should silently make this vow:
"I and all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu* are non-dual in essence with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
However, while I and all sentient beings remain deluded,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have already attained awakening.
I now universally act for the sake of all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm.
Seeking rebirth in the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī,
enter this *bodhimaṇḍa* to recite the sūtra texts and invoke the Buddha’s name,
according to the *Buzhuri* (Supplementary Ritual).
The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* states:
"If one wishes to give rise to the aspiration for rebirth in the Western Land,
one should first visualize the image of the Buddha, one zhang and six chi in height, upon the surface of the water in the pond."
As previously stated, the physical dimensions [of the Buddha] are boundless and beyond the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings;
thus, it is only those at the stage of the ten faiths who are able to perceive the eighty thousand marks and signs.
This is not a realm of perception for the initial mind of an ordinary person;
therefore, one is led to contemplate the body of sixteen feet.
As that body possesses thirty-two marks, it cannot be observed in its entirety.
One must enter through a single mark or excellence;
simply by contemplating the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows, the thirty-two marks will naturally manifest.
If your contemplation becomes fully matured, it is not improper to change the object of focus.
There is nothing improper in observing other bodily marks;
however, if one observes this particular mark, it must be understood with extreme clarity.
This mark is located between the two eyebrows and is white like jade or snow.
It is one zhang and five chi in length and five cun in circumference.
It has eight facets on the exterior and is hollow within.
It spirals to the right in a graceful curve, clearly reflecting the golden countenance with distinct and precise boundaries.
It is pure, luminous, and penetrating, beyond all comparison.
To contemplate this samādhi, one must first understand that all phenomena are mind-only and everything is consciousness-only.
Thus, a sutra says:
The mind encompasses the great void, its measure extending throughout the realms of sand.
It is also said:
"The mind is like a skilled painter."
They construct the various aggregates of the five skandhas;
within all worlds,
there is nothing that is not constructed from the mind.
Thus, the land of Ultimate Bliss— including its dependent rewards such as the jeweled trees, jeweled ground,
and jeweled ponds— as well as the primary rewards of Amitābha’s ocean-like assembly and his body with its thirty-two marks,
are all inherently possessed within my own mind.
All are created by my own mind;
they are not obtained from another nor do they come from without.
Only one who can understand this may then discuss the contemplation of the Buddha within the very mind.
Therefore, it can be said that the Pure Land is solely the mind and its inherent nature is Amitābha.
Thus, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgatas are the Dharma-realm body."
Regarding the passage from "He enters into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings" up to "the eighty secondary marks," Master Tiantai provides two interpretations.
First, it is explained in terms of the mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus;
second, it is explained in terms of the correspondence between understanding and entry.
If the first explanation were absent, contemplation would not be contemplation of the Buddha.
If there were no sequential explanation, then the Buddha would exist outside the mind.
In that case, "the practitioner who enters through understanding" is simply the mind itself;
"the mutual resonance of the Way" is the visualization of the Buddha.
Regarding the explanation that "this mind makes the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha":
from the perspective of practicing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it is said that "the mind makes [the Buddha]";
from the perspective of original endowment, it is said that "it is the mind."
This passage appears in the eighth chapter on the Meaning of Contemplating Images, occurring throughout from beginning to end.
Following this pattern, it should read: "It is the mind that creates the sun; the sun is the mind. And so on, up to:
"It is the mind that creates Śākyamuni; Śākyamuni is the mind," and "It is the mind that creates Mahāsthāmaprāpta; Mahāsthāmaprāpta is the mind."
Thus, throughout the nine grades [of rebirth],
wherever one contemplates according to the object, it is universally the same.
Nevertheless, "contemplating the Buddha by means of the mind" is also termed "contemplating the Buddha in accordance with the mind."
This is explained by taking the mind as it relies upon the Buddha;
that is, it is discussed from the perspective of the mind’s inherent endowment, where "identity" arises precisely because of this endowment.
Each citation presents a single meaning, yet the intent necessarily encompasses both.
Although many have spoken of this contemplation of the object, none have yet reached its true significance.
Now, I shall first cite the ancient explanations to evaluate them, and subsequently set forth its correct meaning.
As for the "Dharma of Pure Awakening," it is said:
To gather the Buddha into one's own mind and then employ contemplation is what is called "contemplating the Buddha.
Now, if it is said that one sends one's thoughts to the Western Land while the objective realm remains in this Eastern land, the object of contemplation is already mistaken;
how then could one be born there? This also conflates direct contemplation of the mind with the practice at hand.
Master Guangzhi said:
"To collect the mind and take refuge in the Buddha is called 'contemplating the Buddha' (guanfo);
this is direct contemplation of the Buddha."
Why did the Patriarch designate "contemplating the mind" as the fundamental principle?
According to the insights of these two masters, one must first realize that all phenomena are mind-only before one can contemplate the mind;
first one must realize that all phenomena are Buddha-only.
Only then can one contemplate the Buddha.
This is equivalent to the direct contemplation of the three paths through constant sitting and other practices;
this constitutes the direct contemplation of the mind and the direct contemplation of the Buddha.
The two masters continued their dispute without end and finally sought a resolution from the Patriarch of Siming.
The Patriarch accepted both schools equally, saying:
"It is not that the Buddha is subsumed within the mind."
This is not a matter of gathering the mind to take refuge in the Buddha;
rather, it is a matter of observing the Buddha by means of the mind.
Why? Because the Pure Land of Amitābha is inherently possessed within my own mind.
Therefore, by relying upon the thirty-two marks of the resultant Buddha,
one perfumes the fundamental nature of the Dharma-body inherently possessed within one's own mind;
once contemplative wisdom is perfected, it will manifest spontaneously.
Therefore, the *Miaozong* states:
"Relying upon that [environment and its inhabitants] to permeate the nature of the mind—
such that the nature of the mind is easily awakened— is precisely this meaning."
Question: Regarding the contemplation of the Buddha by means of the mind, is this solely the object of observation?
Does it also include the subject that observes?
Answer: The single character "contemplation" (guan) refers to the observing subject.
The two characters "mind" (xin) and "Buddha" (fo) constitute the object of contemplation.
If this is so, is this object of contemplation false or is it true?
Answer: The object and contemplation discussed by our school are fundamentally different from all other teachings.
The direct contemplation of the true mind and the true Buddha belongs exclusively to the realm of the Buddhas.
Therefore, all so-called "contemplation of the mind" or "contemplation of the Buddha" belong to the realm of delusion.
The intent is that once delusion is understood, it is itself the truth.
It is not necessary to destroy delusion before revealing truth.
According to the various schools that directly contemplate truth,
it is held that delusion must necessarily be destroyed for the principle of truth to manifest.
This is the meaning of severing the nine [realms] by means of principle.
It precisely destroys the cultivated evils of the nine realms and reveals that the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm is the dharma of cessation.
This then belongs to the partial, prior, and distinct teaching (*biejiao*), and is not the wondrous contemplation of the perfect and sudden (*yuantun*).
Question: Since it is said that one contemplates the Buddha by means of the mind, and the Buddha is a person of fruition (*guoren*), how can he be considered delusory?
If this were false, would the World-Honored One Amitābha then be an ordinary person? Answer:
For a practitioner at the initial stage of the path, as long as external objects have not been forgotten, they perceive the existence of other Buddhas.
That which is not non-forgetfulness is likewise the external sense bases (*āyatana*).
Thus, one knows that the fault lies with oneself; what concern is it of the Buddha?
Question: All observed objects do not transcend the internal or the external.
The mind belongs to the internal, while the Buddha belongs to the external.
Now, it is said that one contemplates the Buddha by means of the mind;
does this not mean that one contemplates both the internal and the external together?
If that were so, one would have to look up at the Buddha while simultaneously bowing the head to reflect upon the mind;
it would be like straddling a doorway or having one's head between two ends of a mouse trap.
Ultimately, how should one apply the mind?
Answer: This is even more difficult to reconcile appropriately.
Now, I shall briefly cite the errors of one school and subsequently set forth the correct principle.
Regarding the first point, my predecessors have stated that the meditative object belongs to external observation while the realm belongs to mind-only.
One must know that this teaching contains two faults.
The first is that it falls directly into the error of observing both the internal and the external simultaneously.
Second, there is the error of conflating the mind that belongs to the realm of mere consciousness with the true mind;
this is because a beginner practitioner must rely upon the deluded mind to contemplate the response-body of Amitābha.
Only by revealing the essence of the true Buddha can one avoid this error.
Although the Patriarchs spoke of "establishing the contemplation of mind-only," this was precisely intended only for the objects created by the deluded mind.
One should embody this through the three contemplations;
only when these contemplations are perfected does the true Buddha manifest.
Thus, one should know that this [other] explanation is profoundly erroneous.
Next, regarding the emergence of the True Principle (Saddharma):
one must understand that my mind is not restricted by spatial location;
this is as stated in the scriptural passage cited previously.
Therefore, Jingxi said:
"The term 'mind-only' does not refer solely to the true mind;
one must understand that the deluded mind of afflictions is also pervasive."
If you do not yet know that the mind of affliction is omnipresent, how can you understand that the form of birth and death is omnipresent? Why?
Because omnipresent form is itself the mind.
If that were so, there would be no need to bring the Buddha back to this eastern land;
nor would there be any need to look up at the Buddha within the substance of the five aggregates while bowing one's head to contemplate the mind.
Now, I shall resolve this:
The meditative state belongs to the external;
yet the object is itself the mind.
There is no need to subsume the Buddha within the mind.
This is what is truly called "contemplating the Buddha by focusing the mind.
To clarify it in this way not only profoundly captures the Buddha’s intent,
but also transcends ordinary worldly understanding.
Moreover, the Buddha personally spoke by way of analogy, saying:
"It is like holding up a bright mirror and seeing the reflection of one's own face;
the image within the mirror is on the outside."
How could it be that only when [the image] is gathered back into my own body would it constitute my likeness?
It is also intended to draw the mind toward that [Buddha-field], serving as the cause for rebirth there.
Although there is no fixed location, due to delusion, one becomes restricted to a specific place.
Now, by using wondrous understanding to harmonize this restricted mind,
one immediately realizes the three truths and three contemplations within the Buddha-nature;
this is the mirror-like analogy for the method of contemplation.
One practices contemplation by grasping the metaphor;
seeing the image is the metaphor for the completion of contemplation,
which is the very sight of the Buddha of one's own original nature.
When the image produced by contemplation has not yet been perfected, it already exists externally;
using this as an analogy for the mind, why must it be drawn back and gathered within one's own body?
This analogy is manifest, yet people themselves fail to understand it.
Question: Regarding the meditative concentration on the Buddha based on the mind, it is external;
the object, therefore, belongs to the realm of delusion.
This meaning is evident and beyond doubt.
To employ the three contemplations to realize this delusive realm as the wondrous Three Truths, I pray you will show their characteristics.
Answer: It is like contemplating the white tuft of hair with single-minded focus, concentrating one's thoughts without wavering.
Clearly and distinctly able to comprehend this object,
which is fully endowed with all dharmas— does this characteristic arise from my body,
or does it arise from my mind?
The Buddha is not obtained from my body;
he is not obtained from my mind;
nor is the Buddha-mind obtained from my body.
One does not attain the form of a Buddha through the mind.
Why is this? If it were the mind, the Buddha would be without mind;
if it were form, the Buddha would be without form.
One cannot seek *sambodhi* through form or mind;
since the object of observation is empty,
the observing subject is likewise quiescent.
When both subject and object are extinguished, one does not fall into conceptual thought;
though emptiness is ungraspable, it is perceived immediately upon recollection,
just as a mirror reflects a face and its image appears therein.
Furthermore, it is like a bhikṣu who contemplates a skeleton emitting various kinds of light;
this has no one to bring it forth, nor does this skeleton exist in reality—
it is all a mental construction.
All are like illusions and transformations, mere fabrications;
the Buddha has never come, and I have nowhere gone.
The mind does not know itself, and the mind cannot see the mind.
When the mind has conceptualization, there is delusion;
non-conceptualization is nirvana.
This dharma cannot be demonstrated.
All are produced by mental conceptualization;
even if such conceptualization exists, it is non-existent and merely empty.
The middle three contemplations are discussed from the perspective of the contemplating subject.
The Three Truths are spoken of from the perspective of what is manifested.
In the contemplation of truth, subject and object are non-dual, being as one.
Thus, the Patriarch said:
The three truths, the three contemplations, and the three non-threes—these threes are each one, and there is nothing to which they can be attached.
Since the names of the truths and contemplations differ while their essence is identical, it is said that the duality of subject and object is in fact non-dual. This is what is meant.
Question: You have stated that the three contemplations within one mind and the three truths within one object constitute the perfect and sudden samādhi, being neither prior nor posterior.
According to what has been discussed above, this seems to follow a sequential order; where, then, lies the meaning of "one mind"?

The answer states: Although the preceding and succeeding functions occur simultaneously, for instance, when one contemplates this white tuft of hair as being one's own mind, there is no phenomenon apart from the mind;
since all phenomena are unobtainable, they are empty.
Its characteristics are clearly illusory;
the illusory is itself the object,
and emptiness is itself the contemplation.
To understand thoroughly and penetrate clearly so as not to be defiled by objects is to transcend the provisional;
to understand thoroughly and penetrate clearly so as not to be purified by wisdom is to transcend emptiness.
It is neither defilement nor purification.

When both object and contemplation are simultaneously transcended and subject and object are instantly extinguished, this is precisely the Middle Way; how could there be any sequence of before and after?
If one discusses the contemplation of the provisional, it is likewise thus.
The white tuft of hair is as if it were raised from the bone; its light is provisional.
Its characteristics cannot be apprehended, for it is empty.
There is nothing here that can be brought forth.
Nor is there any bone that constitutes this "middle.
If one discusses the Middle Way, one realizes that this white curl is neither empty nor provisional;
if the mind harbors conceptualization, it is delusion.
Non-conceptualization is nirvana.
This dharma cannot be demonstrated; it is that which all conceptualizations and perceptions have ceased, thereby transcending the two extremes.
Since both are simultaneously extinguished, there must necessarily be simultaneous illumination.
Because they are illuminated simultaneously, emptiness and the provisional are perfectly distinct;
the cessation of [subjective] illumination and the act of illumination occur at the same time and cannot be sequential.
Thus, when one is empty, all are empty, and the three contemplations are simultaneously empty.
In the one provisional, all are provisional; the three contemplations are all provisional.
In the one middle, all are middle; the three contemplations are all middle.
Without before or after, they transcend thought and transcend discourse.
Question: If the Pure Land is located beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of lands, why do you say it is the Pure Land of the Mind and Amitābha is one’s own original nature?
Furthermore, the sutra states that Amitābha Buddha is not far from here. How can these be reconciled?
Answer: This meaning must be explained by means of the three truths and the three contemplations for the doubt to be resolved.
Why? Because from the perspective of not losing one's own essence, where east and west are distinct and clear, what prevents it from being beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of lands?
This is precisely the wondrous provisional.
From the perspective that the single essence of nature is not separated by even a hair’s breadth,
this is precisely the wondrous empty.
At the point where the two characteristics of neither being identical nor different have vanished and merged,
this is precisely the wondrous Middle Way.
Furthermore, because one is all, there is no hindrance to their being distant.
Because all is one, there is no hindrance to proximity;
because it is neither one nor all, it is neither distant nor near.
By this analogy, one adopts and discards, yet neither adopts nor discards.
The same applies to all things, whether they are combined or dispersed, conjoined or unconjoined, and so forth,
as detailed in the first six chapters of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Relying upon the *Sūtras*, this work extensively expounds sublime understanding to directly discuss the fundamental reality of all phenomena.
There is nothing that is not the wondrous Dharma of the Three Truths.
It is by virtue of this principle of inherent possession (*li-jù*) that phenomenal function (*shi-yòng*) arises;
because it is precisely the provisional (*jiǎ*), its own essence is not lost.
Without traveling far, one is born in that land;
furthermore, because it is emptiness itself and because it is of the same single essence,
this occurs through the power of the Buddha.
Because of the power of samādhi;
because one is able to see [all things] in a single thought-moment;
and because the mind abides in meditative concentration.
Because it is like the snap of a finger, it is neither distant nor near;
in reality, one does not go to rebirth, thereby transcending both extremes of existence and non-existence.
Since the fact that there is neither birth nor non-birth is itself the principle, it is the wondrous reality.
However, because the faculties of those in the Buddha’s world were sharp, mentioning any one of these three necessarily implied the presence of all three.
Thus, the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* speaks specifically of the distant [rebirth],
while the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations* speaks specifically of the near [rebirth].
Since both the distant and the near are simultaneously illuminated, they must both be simultaneously quiescent.
Thus, the near and the distant are neither near nor distant;
arising is non-arising, and non-arising is arising—neither arising nor non-arising.
People today give rise to understanding based on the literal words and become biasedly attached to one side, unable to achieve a comprehensive understanding.
Thus, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* says:
"When people today hear the word 'birth,' they immediately form a conceptualization of birth."
To hear [the teaching] that there is no arising and immediately form the understanding that there is no arising—
this is precisely to fall into such censure. How tragic!
If one does not discuss the three dharmas as being inherently complete according to principle,
but instead discusses them as three dharmas in terms of their functional activity,
then one encounters the error of [the view that] dharmas arise from the mind.

Furthermore, this would incur the criticism of "relying on conditions to sever the nine [stages]," which could hardly be considered a Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) Dharma-gate. If it were not so, [then what is?]
For what reason does the *Miaozong* cite the three powers from the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* as proof?
First, the power of the Buddha;
second, the power of samādhi.
Are these two not functional activities?
Third is the power of fundamental merit;
is this not the inherent endowment?

However, practitioners of the final age who wish to establish their practice and engage in cultivation must select the gateway for entering into principle and the locus from which to initiate contemplation;
this is because sentient beings remain lost in delusion and have not yet awakened to that principle.
Therefore, it is only in the seventh chapter on "Correct Cultivation" that the selection of the objects of observation—
the ten realms such as the aggregates and so forth— is discussed;
the present case is likewise as previously explained.
It is surely because one does not perceive this meaning therein that such confusion arises—is it not so?

Question: How do the "only-mind" (weixin) of the "Pure Land of Only-Mind," the "Original Nature Amitābha," and the "only-form and only-mind" (weise weixin) of the *Ten Gates of Non-duality* differ from one another?
Answer: The Pure Land of Mind-Only is the objective realm of the aggregates to be contemplated;
its fundamental nature is Amitābha.
This revealed dharma-gate is both the object of contemplation and the contemplating subject;
each aspect is cited from one side with the intent of mutual illumination.
If the Ten Non-dual Gates are categorized according to the three truths:
Based on the wondrous nature of form and the wondrous nature of mind, one speaks of "mind-only.
Therefore, it is said that what is neither form nor mind is emptiness;
yet both form and mind are provisional.
It is solely within form and mind.
This is discussed directly in terms of the Middle Way that transcends all opposition;
it is called wondrous form and wondrous mind.
How could this be compared to the contemplation of the mental aggregates (*skandha-citta*) within the Land of Mind-Only?
By carefully examining the *Jin'gang yaozhi*, one will see for oneself the difference between them.
Since the physical characteristics of the two Bodhisattvas are identical, it is all the more necessary to distinguish between them.
The Sūtra says:
"One knows it is Avalokiteśvara by observing only the head;
likewise for Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
As for the Prime Minister:
atop the crown of Avalokiteśvara’s head is a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa),
like an unopened lotus, translucent, pure, red, and fresh.
A great multitude reaches up to the uṣṇīṣa on his head.
There is a precious vase filled with various radiances.
When recollecting the name of this Bodhisattva, one must contemplate this mark.
When recollecting the assembly of the Pure Ocean,
one must visualize the various devas of the Three Vehicles surrounding one Buddha and two Bodhisattvas.
The characteristics of the objects and contemplations discussed herein may all be understood by analogy with what precedes.
If one does not exercise precise discernment, how can it be called "perfect cultivation"?
Therefore, I cannot refrain from further explanation.
I have recorded this as it came to my pen; my old eyes are dim and clouded, so I have not been able to proofread the text, which contains many omissions and errors.
May the reader forgive me.
Written on the third day before the winter solstice in the third year of Zhida.
The Essential Gate to the Contemplation of the Pure Land Realm, Concluded.
